intro: Mendelssohn’s The Hebrides, Op. 26, is a Scottish seascape marked Allegro moderato. It opens with a six-note falling phrase in the violas, cellos and bassoon while the violins hold notes above, and Mendelssohn develops this phrase through the rest of the piece.

sections.label: A · Falling phrase in low strings
sections.mNote: Violas, cellos and bassoon play beneath held violin notes.

sections.label: B · Cellos and bassoons in D
sections.mNote: A broad melody above rippling upper strings

sections.label: C · Running strings, brass and timpani
sections.mNote: Short figures carry the orchestra to the end of the exposition

sections.label: Dev · Wind calls over quiet strings
sections.mNote: The falling phrase passes between instruments and through several keys.

sections.label: A′ · Opening phrase returns, B minor
sections.mNote: Violas and cellos play the opening phrase again.

sections.label: B′ · Clarinet melody in B major
sections.mNote: The broad melody returns over held string chords.

sections.label: Coda · Oboes and running violins
sections.mNote: Animato: short wind phrases over renewed string motion.

sections.label: A″ · Clarinet, flute and pizzicato strings
sections.mNote: The falling phrase is shortened to its last few notes.

relations.label: The lyrical phrase is restated
relations.basis: The lyrical second-subject group in the exposition reiterates its broad phrase over continuing accompanimental motion. Both measured spans lie in the D-major contrast identified near 120 s, not in the later recapitulation. CENS diagonal mean 0.927, sustained 19 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 27 s (cache/form/mendelssohn-hebrides.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening phrase, violas, cellos, bassoon
cues.text: Violas, cellos and first bassoon play a falling phrase in B minor. It starts after a quaver’s rest: F♯, D, C♯, D, B, F♯. Above it, the violins hold two quiet notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, plate M.B. 8, p. 1, bars 1–2. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP122244-PMLP05059-Mendelssohn_-_Die_Hebriden_FS_rsl.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to his family, 7 August 1829
cues.text: On 7 August 1829 Mendelssohn wrote to his family: “In order to make you understand how extraordinarily the Hebrides affected me, the following came into my mind there.” Beneath the words he wrote twenty-one bars of music. He visited Fingal’s Cave the next day.
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn’s letter to his family, 7 August 1829, reproduced and translated by Yale’s Art and Music in Britain exhibition. https://artandmusic.yale.edu/romantic-landscapes/mendelssohn-scotland/mendelssohn-gallery2-letter-his-family

cues.title: Second theme, cellos and bassoons
cues.text: The second theme is in D major, marked cantabile. Cellos and bassoons play it together while the upper strings continue their semiquavers.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 9–10: cantabile theme in bassoons and cellos, with upper-string semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First London performance, 1832
cues.text: The Hebrides was first heard in London on 14 May 1832, on a programme that also included Mendelssohn’s overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream. After the concert he revised the score again.
cues.evidence: Duncan Gillies, Portobello Orchestra programme note, records the London première, the accompanying overture and revision after the performance. https://www.theportobelloorchestra.co.uk/ProgrammeNotes/MendelssohnHebrides.php

cues.title: Development, wind calls over strings
cues.text: In the development, accented wind calls sound above the strings, which play piano and pianissimo. The opening phrase passes through the violas and cellos, sometimes cut to a few notes. The trumpets play a repeated rhythm, marked marcato.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 17–19: wind accents above piano and pianissimo strings; trumpet figures marked marcato.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Turner at Staffa, 1831
cues.text: Turner visited Staffa in 1831. His painting Staffa, Fingal’s Cave shows a steamship passing the island’s basalt cliffs, with smoke and spray in the air. Mendelssohn had been there two years earlier.
cues.evidence: Yale Center for British Art, Staffa, Fingal’s Cave, c. 1831–32, B1978.43.14; the catalogue records Turner’s 1831 visit and the steamer. https://interactive.britishart.yale.edu/critique-of-reason/360/staffa-fingals-cave

cues.title: Return of the opening phrase
cues.text: The falling phrase returns in B minor in the violas and cellos, marked tranquillo, while the violins continue to move above it. This return follows the wind calls and rapid scales of the development.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 29–30: return of the opening phrase in lower strings, marked piano tranquillo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme in B major, clarinets
cues.text: The long second theme returns in B major. The first clarinet plays it above held string chords, marked tranquillo assai (very calm); the second clarinet enters later in the phrase. The moving accompaniment of the first statement is gone.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 32: first clarinet, pianissimo and tranquillo assai, followed by second clarinet; sustained strings beneath.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Animato, in tempo
cues.text: At Animato, in tempo the violins resume their semiquavers and the oboe plays a short staccato phrase. The clarinet’s long melody ends. B minor returns, and the semiquavers spread through the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 33 onwards: Animato in tempo, oboe staccato and renewed semiquavers in the violins.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, clarinet, flute and pizzicato
cues.text: The orchestra reduces. A clarinet plays the falling phrase again and the flute follows with a phrase of its own. The strings close with a few pianissimo pizzicato notes in B minor.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 42: clarinet recollection, flute phrase and final pianissimo pizzicato strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Cellos and bassoons take the long tune
transitions.from: A · Falling phrase in low strings
transitions.to: B · Cellos and bassoons in D
transitions.how: The music reaches D major, the relative major of B minor. The double bass holds a quiet D, and cellos and bassoons begin the new melody, marked cantabile. Violins and violas continue their semiquavers, now marked sempre pp, always very soft.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 8–9, opening of the second subject.

transitions.title: Wind calls over alternating string figures
transitions.from: C · Running strings, brass and timpani
transitions.to: Dev · Wind calls over quiet strings
transitions.how: The D-major closing music breaks off at rehearsal C. Horns and trumpets repeat their clipped rhythm as the strings drop to piano. The violins alternate between two notes while the low strings play the falling phrase again. Wind chords enter fortissimo and diminish at once.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 17–18, rehearsal C and the following wind and string exchanges.

transitions.title: Low strings return to the opening
transitions.from: Dev · Wind calls over quiet strings
transitions.to: A′ · Opening phrase returns, B minor
transitions.how: The rushing scales die away, and the violas and cellos bring back the B-minor opening phrase, marked piano tranquillo. The double bass holds a note beneath them. Above, the violins continue their alternating pairs of notes while the last wind figures die away.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 28–30: diminishing wind figures and the lower strings’ tranquillo return.

transitions.title: Clarinet second theme in B major
transitions.from: A′ · Opening phrase returns, B minor
transitions.to: B′ · Clarinet melody in B major
transitions.how: The strings descend, become quieter and then hold a B-major chord. Over their low B, the clarinet begins the second tune, tranquillo assai. D♯ replaces the D♮ of B minor. The bassoons and cellos played the tune first, and here it passes to the clarinet.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 31–32: descent into the sustained B-major accompaniment and clarinet melody.

transitions.title: Animato, in tempo, after the ritardando
transitions.from: B′ · Clarinet melody in B major
transitions.how: The clarinets slow and diminish over the strings. At Animato, in tempo the violins resume their semiquavers, and the oboe plays a staccato phrase above a held F♯ in the low strings. The harmony turns back towards B minor, and soon afterwards the bass moves again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 33: un poco ritardando, then Animato in tempo, oboe staccato and F♯ in the low strings.

transitions.title: Closing clarinet and flute phrases
transitions.to: A″ · Clarinet, flute and pizzicato strings
transitions.how: The final B-minor passage reduces from full orchestra to a falling phrase in the clarinet and a short phrase in the flute. The strings change to pizzicato, pianissimo. Low B is held in the bass, and a written pause follows the last plucked notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 42, final bars.

source.title: Mendelssohn, The Hebrides (Fingal’s Cave), Op. 26, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke Serie 2, 1874, plate M.B. 8; Partitur-Bibliothek reprint)
source.locator: Opening, p. 1; D-major melody, pp. 9–10; development, pp. 17–29; returning themes, pp. 29–33; closing pages, pp. 33–42.

timeline.note: Violas, cellos and first bassoon play the falling phrase beneath two held violin notes.
Clarinets enter first, then oboes and flutes, holding notes above the moving lower strings.
Horns and trumpets enter as the strings grow louder, over a timpani roll.
The orchestra reaches fortissimo, then the violins’ running notes drop to pianissimo.
Cellos and bassoons play the D-major theme over semiquavers in the upper strings.
Running strings meet short wind and brass figures, with timpani reinforcing the chords.
Wind and horn calls enter over the strings’ quiet, rocking figure.
The woodwinds play short, detached notes above plucked strings.
Winds, brass and running strings play fortissimo above a timpani roll.
The wind phrases grow quieter, and the lower strings return to their falling line, marked tranquillo.
Violas and cellos carry the returning B-minor phrase, with bassoon joining above the low strings.
A clarinet plays in B major over held pianissimo string chords; the second clarinet joins the phrase.
Animato: the violins run again beneath short, detached woodwind phrases.
The strings play fast figures against fortissimo wind and brass chords, with timpani beneath.
The clarinet repeats the falling phrase; a flute follows before the strings’ last plucked notes.

composer.epithet: Composer who wrote a work for eight string players at the age of sixteen.
facts: Ludwig Berger, piano; Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition
Düsseldorf music director, 1833–35; Leipzig Gewandhaus conductor from 1835
Married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children; brother of Fanny Hensel
Leipzig Conservatoire, founded 1843; ten visits to Britain
composer.background:
In 1825 the sixteen-year-old Felix Mendelssohn wrote a birthday present for his violin teacher, Eduard Rietz. It was scored for four violins, two violas and two cellos, and gave Rietz a first-violin part that rises above the other seven players in long arcs. Eleven years later the composer played second viola in a public performance of the E♭ major Octet. Writing to Karl Klingemann on 31 January 1836, he admitted to “heart palpitations”.

Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg on 3 February 1809; the family moved to Berlin two years later. In 1812 his sister Fanny wrote to friends in Hamburg: “Felix has a strong voice and sings all day.” His father Abraham was a banker, his grandfather Moses the Jewish philosopher. Abraham and Lea Mendelssohn had their children baptised as Christians in 1816 and used the additional surname Bartholdy. Fanny and Felix learnt piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter.
